newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr shaken by seismic shift in yen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr shaken by seismic shift in yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished Friday at three month lows as signs of a seismic shift in the Japanese stance on the yen and interest rates struck fear into the heart of high yielding currencies everywhere.

They have benefited hugely from capital inflows as Japanese investors fled record low rates, but all was threatened by a few comments from Japanese officials that the economy was not as weak as it seemed and the yen's long correction might be over.
Exporter and Asian bids cradled the currency at US$0.7820 today, but dealers could not shake the feeling the world had become a less friendly place for the dollar this week.

By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar was lying at US$0.7832/37 after crumbling to US$0.7838/42 late Thursday from an opening US$0.7915/20. That was its worst finish since August 16 and compared with last Friday's close of US$0.7896/01.
It delved as deep as US$0.7815 at one stage as taught market nerves reverbated to rumours of an imminent rate hike from the Bank of Japan, but rallied when the axe failed to fall.

But the loose talk was enough to drive Japanese bond yields sharply higher, so narrowing the dollar's yield premium over the yen only a couple of days after Australia's Reserve Bank had cut official rates by 0.5 point to 6.5 percent.

The dollar had weathered the domestic rate cut with some ease, only to come unstuck when the powerful Japanese Ministry of Finance seemed to suffer a change of heart on its year-old policy of driving the yen lower.
The usually sombre MOF also turned upbeat on the economy, sparking suspicions the authorities were considering raising interest rates, perhaps even as early as today.

This was important for the dollar since low rates there had driven a lot of Japanese money into high yielding A$ samurais, and the resulting panic left it at 87.90/00 yen in late trade after collapsing to 88.05/15 Thursday from an opening 90.20/30.
The full scale of the rout was seen in the dollar's trade weighted index which was down at 57.8 from 58.6 early on Thursday and 58.8 a week ago.
"As afar as the AUD are concerned historically proven fundamental influences are presently in the back seat," said Tim Moloney, an economist at Commonwealth Bank.
"Capital flows from Japan, and the perceptions thereof, are easily the dominant influence at the moment," he said.
The outlook was not all gloom since he thought fears of a Japanese hike were way overdone and, anyway, rates were so low that Australian assets would always enjoy a huge premium.
There had been concerns about investor confidence in the samurai market after Moody's on Thursday highlighted the default risk of some of the issuers.

However, dealers said the impact of the report had faded when it became clear the U.S. ratings agency was only concerned about straight yen-denominated samurais from minor borrowers with low credit ratings.

In contrast yen/A$ dual currency samurai bonds almost always carried high credit ratings and came from sovereign entities like Sweden and Denmark, supra-nationals like the World Bank or major corporates such as French electricity giant EDF.
Dealers said confidence could not have been too badly dented since a 20 bln yen/A$ samurai was successfuly launched for the state of New South Wales today.
However, CBA's Moloney said cracks had begun to appear in the local dollar's resilient edifice.

Commoditiy prices -- long a major determinant of the currency's value -- were putting in a lacklustre performance while speculation of another RBA rate cut would persist for the next few months. "As such, we remain comfortable with our view that the AUD will break toward 77 cents by year end," he said.
